analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 30% minimum tax rate on incomes over $1 million.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2025 with 15 Senate cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a minimum tax on households with income over $1 million a year: they would owe at least 30% of their income after charitable donations, counting regular income tax, payroll tax, and the investment income tax together, and it would phase in starting just above $1 million. The bill says this would cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year and serve as a stepping stone toward broader tax reform. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and the public at large, because the bill would raise billions of dollars a year from the highest-income households, reducing the deficit without raising taxes on anyone earning under $1 million. Middle-income taxpayers would pay nothing new.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a 30% floor on the federal income tax rate for households with income over $1 million a year, counting regular income tax, payroll tax, and the 3.8% net investment income tax together, so households with very high incomes could not fall below that rate.
The tax phases in gradually above the $1 million threshold, so a household just over the line pays only a small share of the full tax, and the threshold rises with inflation after 2025.
The bill preserves the charitable contribution deduction against the minimum tax, so giving to charity does not count against a taxpayer's income.
The bill's own findings section says it would cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year and act as a floor on taxes for the highest-income taxpayers while broader tax reform is debated.

analysis.who_pays: Households with income over $1 million a year, who would owe a new minimum tax equal to the difference between a 30% tax on income after charitable giving and what they currently pay in income and payroll taxes.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates most itemized deductions and many tax credits (it keeps only the foreign tax credit, the earned income credit, and the child credit) in calculating the minimum tax, which would complicate filing for affected households and could raise their bills in ways beyond the headline 30% rate.

Revenue from the tax, described by the bill as billions per year, is small relative to the federal deficit, so the bill alone does not close budget gaps; the bill itself frames it as an interim step, not a full solution.

A minimum tax based on income above $1 million adds a parallel calculation to an already complicated tax code, and opponents of minimum-tax designs generally argue that it adds complexity and could affect some taxpayers inconsistently, such as those with large one-time gains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill raises money from a small group of very high-income households and asks nothing of everyone else, and it phases in above the threshold to avoid cliff effects. The real drawbacks are complexity in the tax code and relatively modest revenue compared with the deficit, which the bill acknowledges by calling itself an interim step toward broader tax reform. On balance it is a targeted tax increase on millionaires, not a broad reform.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Whitehouse and 14 Democratic-aligned cosponsors introduced the bill on April 1, 2025.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced; that referral is the last action in the bill's record.
The bill's tax would apply to tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, and the bill states it would cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with incomes over $1 million, who currently pay no minimum tax beyond today's rates because the bill has not advanced; ordinary taxpayers get no revenue benefit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income households, under current tax rules

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors are Democrats or the chamber's independents; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in the Finance Committee, which is led by the Republican majority that did not act on it.

industries.industry: Households with incomes over $1 million a year
industries.note: The bill would impose a 30% minimum federal tax on their income after charitable giving, closing the gap between their effective tax rate and that of middle-income households. Their interest in stopping the bill runs directly against the revenue benefit to the general public.

industries.industry: Investment fund managers and other high earners whose income comes largely from capital gains and carried interest
industries.note: The minimum tax counts payroll taxes and the net investment income tax toward the 30% floor, reducing the advantage of income taxed at lower capital gains rates. These households benefit most from the current system the bill targets.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and advisory firms serving high-net-worth clients
industries.note: A new parallel minimum tax with its own deductions and credit rules adds planning and compliance work for affected taxpayers, which these firms would be paid to navigate.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or markup rarely move, and this one has the committee's Republican majority to win over first. With a narrower Democratic and independent base of cosponsors than earlier versions of this idea and no scheduled action, the most likely path is that the bill stays in committee unless tax policy becomes a live negotiation where a millionaire minimum tax is traded into a larger package.
